newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr rally falters short of safety.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr rally falters short of safety.

text.p: A beleaguered Australian dollar hung onto 1/2 cent of much-needed offshore gains on a quiet Monday but, crucially, stalled short of safe territory suggesting the downside danger was far from over.
The currency had begun on a high after rallying over 3/4 cent late Friday in a classic bear squeeze, but slowly drooped as Tokyo houses sold AUD/yen and importers went on the offer.

Indeed, the session was dominated by indecision as recent wild swings from 79 cents to a five-month US$0.7740 low and then back to 78, have muddied the chart outlook and left local investors, at least, reluctant to take fresh positions.

By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the dollar was lying in no man's land at US$0.7810/15, between support at US$0.7740 and resistance at US$0.7850. It had faded from an opening US$0.7825/30 but was still well up on Friday's late US$0.7758/63.

Dealers said the sharp short covering squeeze had singed a few fingers amongst the speculators and bought the currency a day or two of grace, but the technical background would remain bleak as long as US$0.7850 capped.
If that were captured there was a gap to be filled back to 79 cents, but otherwise analysts looked for an eventual test of US$0.7720 support on route to the August low of US$0.7680.
On the crosses the currency was up on Friday's weak finish, but again off its early peaks on a lack of follow up demand.
On the yen it rallied to 90.70/80 yen from a 89.02/02 close Friday, while growing expectations of a rate cut in Germany lifted it to 1.2383/98 marks from 1.2236/50.
In trade weighted terms it firmed to 58.4 from 58.0.

Dealers reported some talk of more yen/A$ dual currency bonds in the pipeline after a couple last week, but the chatter was not as loud as last week and there was a feeling Japanese investor interest might be drifting toward samurais denominated in U.S. or Canadian dollars.
That partly reflected the growing belief the next move in U.S. interest rates would be upwards in the wake of a strong 262,000 rise in payrolls for December, reported last week.
In contrast Australian policy monetary could well be eased again this quarter, the fourth move since last July.

The risk of another cut here was considered evenly balanced by analysts -- the latest Reuter poll of 30 economists came out with a percentage chance of exactly 50 percent -- but may become a little clearer after key jobs data are released on Thursday.
The figures are expected to show employment growth slowed to 5,000 in December from 24,400 the month before.
That rate of growth was not enough to compensate for new entrants to the jobs market so the unemployment rate was seen inching up to 8.6 percent from 8.5 percent in November.

Estimates for this volatile series range from a 15,000 rise to a 25,000 fall, and anything like the latter will put markets on red alert for an easing and undermine the dollar's already shaky support.

Also due this week were housing finance commitments for November and Janurary consumer confidence which should provide some clue to how consumers were responding to the rate cuts already delivered. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
